title: Counting
hookLine: an old method: count breaths from one to ten, then begin again

cards: Sometimes it goes like this. You sit down to watch the breath. Three breaths in, you're planning dinner.
Then you're rehearsing an argument. Then you're wondering if you left the stove on. Five minutes later you remember: oh, right, the breath.
Sixteen beautiful steps are no use if you can't stay for two. So the old teachers gave beginners something simpler to hold on to, something any child can do. They count.

teach.h: ONE TO TEN, THEN BEGIN AGAIN.
teach.b: The Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, describes counting, ganana, as the very first stage of breath meditation for a beginner. Breathe in, breathe out: one. Breathe in, breathe out: two.
Up to ten, then back to one. And if you lose count, which you will, you also go back to one.

teach.h: NOT BELOW FIVE, NOT PAST TEN.
teach.b: The manual is oddly specific about the numbers: don't stop below five, and don't go beyond ten. Count only to three or four, and the mind feels cramped and restless, like cattle shut in a pen that's too small.
Count past ten, and the mind starts paying attention to the numbers instead of the breath. Five to ten is the sweet spot: long enough to settle, short enough to stay with.
Once the mind can stay with the breath without the counting, the manual says, you let the counting go.
It's scaffolding, not the building. And counting isn't found only in this one manual; some Zen and Tibetan teachers count breaths with beginners too. Here's the part that matters most.
Losing count isn't failure. It's the practice.
Every time you notice you've drifted off to dinner plans and go back to one, that noticing is the muscle getting stronger. Reaching ten isn't the goal, and missing it isn't a mark against you.
Whatever happens, the instruction stays the same, with no scolding at all.

how: Counting breaths from one to ten is a beginner's method described in the Visuddhimagga and also used by some Zen and Tibetan teachers, with the instruction to begin again at one whenever the count is lost.

games.q: you're counting breaths and suddenly realize you're at fourteen. what do you do?
games.why: back to one, with no scolding. the noticing is what strengthens the mind.

practice: Let the breath be natural, and after each out-breath count silently, one, two, up to ten, then begin again at one.

If you lose track, or catch yourself at fourteen, just smile and go back to one; try for three rounds if time allows, and if you only reach three, that's fine too. The counting is a handrail: keep one hand on it.

wordCard.voice: Counting. An old method for a wandering mind: count breaths from one to ten, and begin again.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: counting; the first stage of breath meditation in the Visuddhimagga.

carryVoice: Your line: back to one. One is always there to come back to. Day one hundred and fourteen, in the books.
